name: StandardAero, Inc.

profile.description: StandardAero is the largest independent pure-play aerospace engine aftermarket services provider, offering engine maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO), on-wing support, component repair and engineering solutions across commercial, business aviation, military and helicopter markets. Founded in 1911, it services platforms including CFM56, LEAP, PT6, and Rolls-Royce engines. It listed on the NYSE in October 2024 after Carlyle ownership; Paul McElhinney succeeded long-time CEO Russell Ford on October 1, 2026.

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Under Russell Ford, revenue grew from $1.6B in 2013 to over $6B in 2025, mainly by scaling existing MRO lines and adding OEM-authorized engine programs; this is execution rather than a transformative pivot [3]. AI Deployment (0/2): No AI-powered customer products or quantified AI-driven efficiency savings were found in earnings materials or company disclosures [1][5]. Market Share (2/2): StandardAero is the largest independent engine MRO provider, with OEM licenses on CFM56, LEAP, and PT6, and posted a record 14.4% adjusted EBITDA margin in Q2 2026 [1][2]. Pipeline (1/2): The LEAP program turned profitable in 2026 and management targets about $1B of annual LEAP revenue by decade-end, but this is a ramp of an existing program rather than a new product [5]. R&D Intensity (1/1): Spending on certifications, tooling, and repair-development capability is in line with independent-MRO peers, whose formal R&D spend is minimal [7].

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): The purpose of keeping the world's engines flying safely and reliably is clear and has endured for 115 years, but it describes the operational mandate shared by every MRO shop rather than a distinctive higher cause [7]. Community Impact (1/2): The 2025 sustainability report cites $1.3M in energy and waste savings and a 45%-by-2030 carbon-reduction goal, but no quantified community or charitable program was found [4]. Employee Retention (1/2): The report says the safety incident rate is 50% better than the industry average, and the planned succession from Ford (CEO since 2013) to Lead Independent Director McElhinney shows continuity, but no turnover or tenure data is disclosed [3][4]. Insider Buying (0/2): No meaningful open-market insider purchases were identified in the last 12 months, following post-IPO secondary sales by Carlyle.

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored as a Growth stock on all seven metrics (total weight 10). D/E of 93.2% scores 0.90 (x1); ROE of 12.3% scores 0.82 (x2); MRQ revenue growth of 4.6% scores 0.82 (x1); 5yr revenue CAGR of about 15% (roughly $3.0B in 2020 to over $6B in 2025) scores 1.0 (x2); Forward P/E of 12.78 scores 1.0 (x1); profit margin of 5.12% scores 0.26 (x1); and Forward PEG of about 0.64 (12.78 forward P/E over ~20% expected EPS growth, consistent with the 24% Q2 adjusted EPS gain) scores 1.0 (x2) [1][3][6]. Weighted sum 8.61/10 = 8.6, rounding to 9; the thin MRO pass-through margin is the main drag. Liquidity floor cleared: 3.53M avg shares x $22.42 = $79.2M daily dollar volume [6].

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): Engine overhaul is physical, regulated work: teardown, inspection, repair, and reassembly in FAA/EASA-certified shops by licensed technicians, with shop-visit intervals driven by flight cycles and regulation [7]. Analyst commentary on the stock centers on LEAP/CFM56 margin inflection and supply-chain execution, not AI substitution [3], and AI-driven predictive maintenance tends to route more targeted work to MRO shops rather than replace them. AI Opportunity (0/1): No AI-attributable revenue or AI service offering is disclosed [1].

infinite_game.summary: StandardAero has kept a single operational purpose, keeping engines flying, through 115 years, several ownership changes, and a 2024 IPO, and its 2026 CEO hand-off was orderly [3]. Through Sinek's lens, though, the private-equity heritage, leverage, and guidance-driven narrative point to a well-run finite operator with infinite-game durability, not a Just Cause company.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): The aviation-safety purpose has outlasted every owner from the 1911 founding through Carlyle and the public listing, which shows a cause that endures beyond any single leader [3][7]. It is more an operational mandate than an idealistic future state that people would sacrifice for, so it falls short of a full Sinek Just Cause.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Management absorbed years of LEAP start-up losses and exited low-margin pass-through revenue, which trimmed reported Q2 2026 growth to 4.6%, in favor of higher-quality earnings [1][5]. Beyond that, capital allocation is focused on deleveraging and meeting raised guidance rather than costly long-term bets.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (1/2): Leadership continuity is strong: Ford led for 13 years and stays as Executive Chairman through 2026 to hand over to McElhinney, who knew the business as Lead Independent Director [3]. The reported safety record (incident rate 50% better than industry) suggests a disciplined shop-floor culture, but no retention or engagement data shows exceptional trust [4].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): The company has moved from legacy turboprop and military overhaul into next-generation commercial platforms (LEAP), component repair, and engineering services, and moved from private to public ownership [5][7]. These are incremental extensions of the engine-MRO model rather than a reinvention.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Earnings commentary emphasizes StandardAero's scale and position against OEM-owned and airline-affiliated shops (GE, Lufthansa Technik, MTU) rather than lessons learned from them [5]. No evidence was found of rivals framed as a source of improvement.

investment_thesis: StandardAero is the scale leader in independent engine MRO, a non-discretionary, regulation-driven aftermarket that grows with the global flight-hour base. Q2 2026 revenue rose 4.6% to $1.60B, while adjusted EBITDA rose 12.3% to a record $230M (14.4% margin) and adjusted EPS rose 24% to $0.40 [1]. Management raised 2026 guidance to $885-910M of adjusted EBITDA and $1.50-1.57 of adjusted EPS [1][5]. LEAP has turned profitable and targets about $1B of annual revenue by decade-end as the largest narrowbody fleet enters heavy shop visits [5]. At a 12.8x forward P/E and an implied PEG near 0.6, with Infrastructure scoring 9/10 and AI risk negligible, the risk/reward is attractive for a business with decades of embedded demand [6].
thesis_continued: The bear case is margin and leverage. GAAP profit margin is only 5.1% because of material pass-throughs, and D/E of 93% reflects the Carlyle-era debt load, leaving less cushion in a flight-hour downturn [6]. Top-line growth slowed sharply from 13.3% in Q1 to 4.6% in Q2 2026, and military/helicopter revenue fell 3% on input delays [1][2]. The new CEO takes over amid persistent supply-chain part shortages, and Sustainalytics rates ESG risk as severe (42.2), an overhang for some institutional holders [4]. The stock sits well below its 52-week high, showing the market is not yet paying for the LEAP ramp.
key_catalysts: LEAP heavy-shop-visit ramp: the program turned profitable in 2026, and management targets about $1B of annual LEAP revenue by decade-end [5]
Delivery on the raised 2026 guidance ($885-910M adjusted EBITDA, $1.50-1.57 adjusted EPS) at Q3/Q4 results, which would confirm the margin expansion after the exit from pass-through revenue [1]
Continued deleveraging, plus possible M&A or capital-return optionality under new CEO Paul McElhinney, former head of GE Aviation Services [3]
key_risks: Revenue growth slowed from 13.3% (Q1) to 4.6% (Q2 2026); a further slowdown or a fall in commercial flight hours could compress the 12.8x forward multiple [1][2]
Supply-chain part shortages and military input delays (military/helicopter revenue down 3% in Q2) constrain shop throughput and turn times [1]
First-year execution risk under a new CEO after Russell Ford's 13-year tenure, combined with 93% D/E that limits flexibility in a downturn [3][6]
